title: Holiday Cocoa Promotions (ANOVA)
text: Teton Pantry Co. sells a 12 oz. Holiday Cocoa through five retailers in four regions. Regional managers disagreed about whether promotions should be deeper in some regions than others. Do promotion depth and region change weekly revenue, and does the effect of a promotion depend on the region?

title: Holiday Cocoa Promotions (ANOVA)
text:
About this project
This was a role-play consulting exercise for MATH 325. The client emails, the sales data (2022 to 2024), and the cover image were generated with ChatGPT 5.1. My replies to the client and the full analysis are my own. ChatGPT was also used to help debug code, customize the graphs, and choose the statistical test.

title: Holiday Cocoa Promotions (ANOVA)
text:
Approach
I built the report in R (car, tidyverse, pander).

Calculated revenue per retailer-week as units sold times actual price.
Grouped promotion depth into three levels: none (0%), small (10 to 25%), and medium (25 to 35%).
Fit a two-way ANOVA with interaction on log revenue: log(revenue) ~ promo + region + promo:region. The log transform stabilizes the variance of the revenue data.

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Measuring the Price of Promotion: A Store-Level Analysis of Consumer Expenditure
Erral Asper, Kathryn Haroldsen, Taylor Landini, Mary Palmer, and Harrison Thomas (April 2026)

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Question
Does promotional advertising push the prices consumers pay up or down? Economic theory points both ways: price-focused promotions can intensify competition, while brand-building advertising can reduce price sensitivity and support higher prices.

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Data
We used the Dominick’s Finer Foods scanner database, compiled by the University of Chicago Booth School of Business from about 100 grocery stores from 1989 to 1994, and focused on the frozen dinner category.

Unbalanced panel of 19,306 store-item units over weeks 1 to 255, for 1,645,316 observations
Removed observations flagged as unreliable, prices of $0, and prices above $6 (over 99% of the data fell below that cutoff)
Promotions coded as Bonus Buy, Coupon, or Simple Price Reduction, compared with weeks with no recorded promotion

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Method
Fixed effects regression with store-item fixed effects, so that each product in each store is compared only against itself across weeks. Model 1 regresses price on the three promotion types. Model 2 adds the retailer’s profit margin.

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Findings
Relative to non-promotion weeks, average prices were lower by:



Promotion type
Average price difference




Bonus Buy
$0.11


Simple Price Reduction
$0.46


Coupon
$0.95




Coupons were the deepest discount and also produced the highest median sales volume.
Adding profit (Model 2) shrank the promotion coefficients to near zero. Because profit depends directly on price, we treated it as endogenous and based our conclusions on Model 1.
A Breusch-Pagan test (BP = 830.21, p < 0.01) found heteroskedasticity, so we used robust standard errors. Variance inflation factors near 1.0 showed no multicollinearity.

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Limitations
The data are observational, cover one retailer and one time period, and record promotions imperfectly, so the results should not be read as causal or applied directly to modern online retail.

title: Merger Sales Dashboard
text:
What the data shows

Revenue growth has flattened. Total revenue across the period is $66.12M with $30.19M in gross profit and an average profit of $226.26 per sale. Quarterly revenue climbed from 2019 through 2022, which is why the page reads “profitable but plateauing.”
Margins are healthy but uneven. Gross profit margin rose from about 40% in 2019 to about 46% by the end of 2022, while clothing profit margins stood out as a concern.



Younger customers drive sales. AdventureWorks’ main demographic is males ages 20 to 30, which lines up with GoBig’s customer base. Millennials and Gen Z lead revenue, although Gen Z revenue peaked in 2022 and has since fallen back below Millennials.



Bikes carry the business. Bikes generate the most revenue and profit even with lower inventory, and they turn over inventory far faster than components.

Every piece, book, and composer on a given shelf, using a five-table join.
The average difficulty of each piece across all of its parts, using AVG and GROUP BY.

SELECT bhp.book_id AS "Book ID", b.book_title AS "Book Title", COUNT(*) AS "Num. of Pieces"
FROM book_has_piece AS bhp
  JOIN book AS b ON bhp.book_id = b.book_id
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 3 DESC;

import datetime as dt

def thanksgiving(y):
    first = dt.date(y, 11, 1)
    first_thu = first + dt.timedelta(days=(3 - first.weekday()) % 7)  # Monday = 0
    return first_thu + dt.timedelta(weeks=3)

def clip_off(n, lo, hi):
    return str(n) if lo <= n <= hi else "none"

def holiday_lookup(dates):
    rows = []
    for d in dates:
        tg = (d - thanksgiving(d.year)).days
        xm = min(((d - dt.date(y, 12, 25)).days for y in (d.year - 1, d.year)), key=abs)
        rows.append((d, "tg_" + clip_off(tg, -3, 4), "xm_" + clip_off(xm, -3, 7)))
    return pl.DataFrame(rows, schema=["date", "tg_off", "xm_off"], orient="row")

categorical_cols = ["month", "weekday", "weathersit", "season", "year", "hr"]

# Recency weights: oldest rows get 0.5, newest rows get 1.0 (raise the 0.5 floor for less emphasis)
days_all = (df["dteday"].str.to_date("%m/%d/%Y") - START).dt.total_days().to_numpy()
w = (0.5 + 0.5 * days_all / days_all.max()).astype("float32")

X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val, w_train, w_val = train_test_split(
    X, y, w, test_size=0.2, random_state=48
)

# min/max scaling lives inside the model, so a holdout is scaled with the training min/max
x_min = X_train.min(axis=0)
x_rng = X_train.max(axis=0) - x_min
x_rng[x_rng == 0] = 1.0   # avoid dividing by zero on constant columns
norm = keras.layers.Rescaling(scale=1.0 / x_rng, offset=-x_min / x_rng)
y_min, y_max = y_train.min(), y_train.max()
y_norm = keras.layers.Rescaling(scale=y_max - y_min, offset=y_min)   # inverse: back to riders

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input(shape=(X_train.shape[1],)),
    norm,
    Dense(150, activation="relu"),
    Dropout(0.4),
    Dense(32, activation="relu"),
    Dropout(0.2),
    Dense(1),
    y_norm,
])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.0008),
              loss="mse", metrics=["mae", keras.metrics.R2Score(name="r2")])
early_stop = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=7,
                                           restore_best_weights=True)
history = model.fit(
    X_train, y_train.reshape(-1, 1),
    sample_weight=w_train,
    validation_data=(X_val, y_val.reshape(-1, 1)),
    epochs=30, batch_size=80, callbacks=[early_stop],
)

title: Bike Rental Demand
text:
Cleaning and features

Split the date into day, month, and year, and combined casual and registered riders into one total.
Added days from Thanksgiving and days from Christmas, which raised R² on a small holdout by about 0.10.
Added a COVID flag for March 2020 through December 2021.
Scaled features with min-max scaling so variables like windspeed (0 to 70) and rider counts (0 to 1,000+) start on equal footing. Z-score scaling gave almost the same result.

A mistake that taught us something: our first model scored nearly 100% because we forgot to remove the casual and registered columns after adding them together, so the model had simply learned to add. We caught it because the result was too good, removed the columns, and rebuilt.

title: Bike Rental Demand
text:
Model
A neural network with two hidden layers using ReLU activations: 150 nodes with 40% dropout, then 32 nodes with 20% dropout. Dropout guards against overfitting. We trained on mean squared error with a batch size of 80, a learning rate of 0.0008, and early stopping with patience of 7. Training stopped at 48 of a possible 100 epochs once the validation error stopped improving, and we kept the weights from the best epoch.

We also tried training on November and December alone, on the theory that holidays behave differently, but there was not enough data to make an accurate model.

text:
Recommendations

Plan for rush hours. Weekday demand peaks at 8 am and 5 pm, while weekends are a smooth midday curve, so renting the same number of bikes at the same hours on weekends would lose revenue.
Expect growth over years, not months. Demand dips every year in November and December, but the long-run trend in D.C. is rising.
Supply fewer bikes around holidays. Thanksgiving week should run slightly below other November weeks, and Christmas week should look like a series of weekends with far fewer riders.

Banco Federal de Finanças had just finished an ineffective telemarketing campaign. The bank asked us to show how machine learning could improve who gets called in future campaigns. We had three goals:

identify the factors most associated with a customer subscribing
build a model that finds the customers most likely to respond

title: Bank Telemarketing Targeting
text:
Approach
We trained a supervised decision tree on about 37,000 records from the previous campaign, with 70% for training and 30% (about 11,100 customers) held out for testing. The features fall into three groups: customer demographics, contact and timing details (including economic indicators), and the outcome of earlier campaigns. The target was whether the customer subscribed.

The two strongest predictors were the bank’s quarterly number of employees (nr.employed) and the 3-month Euribor rate (euribor3m). Both describe the economy when the customer was contacted, so the state of the economy was the best predictor of whether a customer would say yes. The month of contact ranked fourth, which surprised us and which the model cannot explain on its own.

Only about 11.4% of customers subscribed, so a model that always predicted “no” would score 88.7% accuracy and find nobody. We trained with balanced class weights on purpose, which lowers accuracy but finds subscribers. The model found 848 of the 1,262 subscribers in the test set (67.2%). About one in three customers it flagged actually subscribed, which is roughly 2.8 times the random rate of one subscriber in nine calls. The cost is 1,780 calls to customers who did not subscribe.

title: Bank Telemarketing Targeting
text:
Other findings

Prior contact: the share of customers who said yes was about the same whether or not they had been contacted before, so earlier outreach did not appear to backfire.
Privacy: the data contains no names, birth dates, locations, government identifiers, contact details, or account specifics, so it is consistent with GDPR.
Limits: the data is historical and the economic features are correlated with each other, so the model should be retrained as conditions change. Adjusting the classification threshold or tree depth would shift the balance between missed subscribers and wasted calls.

title: King County Housing Prices
text: A client in the housing and insurance space asked for a model that predicts home prices in King County, Washington, using sales from January 2014 to December 2015. The data includes bedrooms, bathrooms, floors, living area, lot size, year built, renovation year, view, waterfront, and a construction grade.

title: King County Housing Prices
text:
Cleaning and features

Split the sale date into separate month and year features and dropped the day, which did not help the model.
Kept the construction grade (1 to 13) as a number instead of binning it. The model improved because grade is an ordered ranking.
Built distance from the center of Seattle, house age, and years since renovation.
Tested the 30-year mortgage rate from FRED and left it out because it did not improve predictive power.
Took the log of price. Raw prices are heavily right-skewed, so a few very expensive homes would dominate the error. The log shifts the model toward minimizing percentage error, and predictions are converted back to dollars afterward.

title: King County Housing Prices
text:
Model
We used XGBoost, an ensemble of gradient-boosted decision trees where each tree corrects the errors of the ones before it. Our first 30% test split turned out to be biased toward homes without basements, so we switched to 5-fold cross-validation, which trains and tests the model five times on different slices and averages the results.

About 90% of the variation in prices was explained on data held out during cross-validation. About 32% of predictions landed within 5% of the true price, 57% within 10%, and 83% within 20%.

Error grows for expensive homes, with accuracy dropping above about $1.5M, because there are few of them to learn from.

Grade was by far the strongest feature (importance 0.37), followed by latitude, living area, waterfront, and view. A geographic cluster covering high-end downtown Seattle was also important.

title: King County Housing Prices
text:
Recommendations

Present estimates as a range instead of a single number.
Manually review extreme high-priced outliers.
Include distance from a major city in future models.

We also declined a request to lower estimates in low-income areas to protect insurance customers. That would have required confidential personal data and would have compromised the model’s integrity. The model already reflects neighborhood conditions through features like the living area of the 15 nearest homes.

Part 4: Visualization
Now that we have explored and preprocessed our data, let’s create a visualization to summarize our findings.

Exploration vs Presentation
Broadly speaking, there are two types of visualizations: * Barebones visualizations you might use to get a quick, visual understanding of the data while you’re trying to decide how it all fits together. * Presentation-quality visualizations that you would include in a report or presentation for management or other stakeholders.


Visualization Tools
There are many different visualization tools availble. In the sections below, we’ll explore the three most common. Each of these libraries has strengths and weaknesses.
It is probably a good idea for you to become familiar with each one, and then become proficient at whichever one you like the best.


Let’s Plot
The Let’s Plot visualization library uses a grammer of graphics to build up a chart piece by piece.
Assume we have a polars dataframe called employees, with three columns: name, job, salary.
# Make a box plot style categorical plot showing the distribution of salaries for each job:
ggplot(data=employees, aes(x='job', y='salary')) + geom_box()

# Make a box plot style categorical plot, and customize the results
(
    ggplot(data=employees, aes(x='job', y='salary'))
    + geom_boxplot()
    + labs(
        title='Salaries by Job Title'
    )
)
Dependencies need to be installed in colab to use Let’s Plot. Use %pip to install it. %pip install lets-plot will install the library, and skip it if it’s already installed.

%pip install lets-plot

from lets_plot import *

Let’s create a barchart showing the count of each movie rating by using Let’s Plot’s capabilities.
In this example, we see the x axis being set to a feature called species, and the y axis is a count of the number of rows for that species.
In our case, we want the x-axis to be set to rating.

Altair
The Altair visualization library provides a large variety of very easy to use statistical charting tools.
Altair uses a declarative language to build up charts piece by piece.
Assume we have a pandas dataframe called employees, with three columns: name, job, salary.
# Make a box plot style categorical plot showing the distribution of salaries for each job:
alt.Chart(employees).mark_boxplot().encode(
    x='job',
    y='salary'
)

# Make a box plot style categorical plot, and customize the results
alt.Chart(employees).mark_boxplot().encode(
    alt.X('job', title='Job title'),
    alt.Y('salary', title='Annual salary in thousands of $USD')
).properties(
  title='Salaries by Job Title'
)

Seaborn
While Altair uses a “declarative” syntax for building charts piece by piece, the Seaborn library provides a large variety of pre-made charts for common statistical needs.
These charts are divided into different categories. Each category has a high-level interface you can use for simplicity, and then a specific function for each chart that you can use if you need more control over how the chart looks.
Seaborn uses matplotlib for its drawing, and the chart-specific functions each return a matplitlib axes object if you need additional customization.
For example, there are several different types of categorical plots in seaborn: bar plots, box plots, point plots, count plots, swarm plots, etc…
Each of these plots can be accessed using the catplot function.
Assume we have a pandas dataframe called employees, with three columns: name, job, salary.
# Make a box plot style categorical plot showing the distribution of salaries for each job:
sns.catplot(data=employees, x='job', y='salary', kind='box')

# Make a swarm plot style categorical plot
sns.catplot(data=employees, x='job', y='salary', kind='swarm')
Alternatively, you can use the plot specific functions to give yourself more control over the output by using matplotlib functions:
# Make a box plot style categorical plot, and customize the results
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 9))
ax = sns.boxplot(data=employees, x='job', y='salary')
ax.set_title("Salaries by Job Title")
ax.set_ylabel("Annual salary in thousands of $USD")
ax.set_xlabel("Job title")

title: Python: Confidence vs. Retail Sales

What the program does

Reads the two CSV files into dictionaries keyed by date and merges them into one compound dictionary.
Validates the user’s input: the dates must parse as “Month, Year”, differ from each other, fall in order, and exist in the data.
Builds the date range and calculates each series’ percent change between the two dates.
Calculates the mean, standard deviation, and the Pearson correlation coefficient with NumPy.
Translates the correlation into a plain-English conclusion, from “almost no correlation” to “very strong correlation.”
Prints a formatted summary table with tabulate.

def write_conclusion(correl_coef):

    elif abs_correl_coef <= 0.29:
        conclusion = "There is a very weak correlation between retail sales and CCI in the given time period."

title: Weather Regression
text: My family has lived in both Arizona and Washington, so I pulled daily weather data (NOAA’s Global Surface Summary of the Day, through the GSODR package) for April 2023 from Phoenix Goodyear Airport and Renton Municipal Airport. How well does the daily minimum temperature predict the daily maximum, and does that relationship differ between the two cities?

title: Weather Regression
text:
Model
\[
\hat{Y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \beta_3 X_{i1} X_{i2}
\]
where \(Y\) is the daily maximum temperature, \(X_1\) is the daily minimum temperature, and \(X_2\) is an indicator for Renton (Phoenix is the baseline). The \(\beta_2\) term lets the lines start at different heights, and the \(\beta_3\) interaction lets them have different slopes.
weather_lm_full <- lm(MAX ~ MIN + AIRPORT + MIN:AIRPORT, data = weather)

In Phoenix, each 1°C rise in the minimum goes with about a 0.91°C rise in the maximum.
In Renton, the line starts about 9.9°C lower, and the slope is steeper at about 1.35°C per 1°C.

I checked all five regression assumptions (linearity, normal errors, constant variance, fixed X, and independent errors) with residual plots and judged the model appropriate. The result matches what the climates would suggest: Phoenix is hotter than Renton in April, and the minimum temperature carries more of the day’s range in Renton.
